message:
I'm redoing our downstairs bathroom floor myself (first time, slightly terrified) and I've got a pile of questions.

The tile shop guy talked really fast so I didn't catch half of it. Could you explain what "lippage" means in tiling, in simple terms? And what's a sensible grout colour for a pale grey porcelain tile if I don't want it looking dirty after a month? My partner also wants to know whether we should do the floor before or after the new toilet goes in, just a quick answer with a reason.

The floor is 2.4 m by 1.8 m. The tiles I like are 30 cm × 60 cm and come in boxes of 8. Everyone online says to add 10% for cuts and breakages. How many boxes do I actually need to buy?

I also need a short, polite message to the neighbours saying there'll be some noise from cutting tiles on Saturday morning, since they've already put up with a skip on the drive for a fortnight. Finally, any three tips for a beginner laying their first floor would be very welcome. I've watched a lot of videos, but they all make it look far easier than it probably is.

Thank you, honestly.
response:
Happy to help. Here's everything in order.

## What "lippage" means

Lippage is when the edge of one tile sits higher than the edge of the tile next to it, so you get a little ridge you can see and feel (and can stub a toe on).

It matters for your tiles because long rectangular tiles like 30 × 60 cm are often very slightly bowed in the middle. Two things help:
- **Use a ⅓ offset, not a ½ offset**, if you're laying them in a staggered (brick) pattern. Putting the middle of one tile next to the end of another exaggerates the bow.
- **Use a tile levelling clip system.** It's cheap, and it holds neighbouring edges flush while the adhesive sets.

## Grout colour for pale grey porcelain

Go for a **mid grey, a shade or two darker than the tile**. It hides the everyday grime that turns pale grout dingy within weeks, and it still looks tidy against the tile. Avoid white or very light grey on a floor.

For a bathroom, a **stain-resistant or epoxy-modified grout** is worth the small extra cost. If you use standard cement grout, seal it once it has cured.

## Floor before or after the toilet?

**Floor first, toilet after.** You tile one continuous floor without cutting around the toilet's curved base, the toilet sits on a level tiled surface, and you can replace the toilet later without leaving an untiled patch.

## How many boxes

**Buy 4 boxes (32 tiles).**

- Floor area: 2.4 × 1.8 = **4.32 m²**
- One tile: 0.3 × 0.6 = 0.18 m², so the floor takes **24 tiles**
- Plus 10%: 26.4, so **27 tiles**
- At 8 per box: 3 boxes gives 24 tiles, which is too few. 4 boxes gives 32.

The 24 is the bare minimum. On paper the room fits the tiles almost exactly, but in practice you'll still need cuts: grout gaps take up space, walls are never perfectly square, and you'll cut around the toilet waste pipe and the doorway. A staggered pattern adds more cuts. The spare 5 or so tiles are useful, and it's worth **keeping two or three after the job** for future repairs.

Also check that all boxes have the **same batch or shade number** on the label. Batches can differ slightly in colour.

## Message to the neighbours

> Hi both, just a quick heads-up that we'll be cutting tiles on Saturday morning for the bathroom floor, so there'll be some noise for a few hours. We'll aim to start no earlier than 9 and finish by lunchtime. Thank you for being so patient with the skip on the drive these past two weeks. It should be gone very soon. Please do knock if anything's a problem.

Adjust the times to whatever you actually plan.

## Three beginner tips

1. **Get the base right before anything else.** The subfloor must be solid, flat and clean. If it's a timber floor, it needs a rigid layer such as tile backer board or exterior plywood screwed down well, or the tiles and grout will crack. Most failed DIY floors fail here, not in the tiling.
2. **Dry-lay the whole floor first.** Lay the tiles out with spacers before mixing any adhesive. Shift the layout so you don't end up with thin slivers at the doorway or along the most visible wall, and mark your starting lines in pencil. Twenty minutes of planning saves most of the frustration later.
3. **Work in small sections and check as you go.** Mix small batches of adhesive and spread only about 1 m² at a time. Press and slightly twist each tile into place. Every few tiles, lift one to check it's fully covered with adhesive underneath, and check it's level with its neighbours. Wipe adhesive off the tile faces and out of the joints before it sets.

The videos make it look easy because it's being done by people who've laid hundreds of floors. Going slowly and checking often is the right way to do your first one, and a 4.3 m² floor is a very manageable first project. Good luck!
